To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

genetic differences in the alcohol exposed fetus' susceptibility or resistance to the long term effects of alcohol in uterine environment, as well as maternal and paternal genetic factors, contribute to variations in the severity of FASD symptoms.

the maternal and paternal alleles can interact to modulate the effects of prenatal alcohol exposure in the offspring, and that this interaction can occur via epigenetic mechanisms that alter the expression of the maternal and paternal genes.
the maternal genetic and hormonal contributions to the alcohol-induced developmental deficits can be the major contributing mechanism to the variations in symptomology of the alcohol-exposure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that underlie the non-Mendelian genetic contributions to FASD symptomology and the interactions between the genetic and epigenetics that influence these phenotypes.

understanding how genetic and epigenetics contribute to the phenotypic variability of FASD and how this variability can be used to identify the mechanisms that lead to the disease and to the development of new therapeutic strategies to prevent and/or reverse the symptoms of FASD.

the mechanisms that lead to the variations in the severity of the phenotypes associated with prenatal alcohol exposure, and how these mechanisms interact with each other to modulate the severity of FASD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
genetic and epigenetics interact to modulate the susceptibility and resilience to FAD.
maternal genetics and epigenetics are the driving forces behind the phenotypes of the alcohol-exposure in the offspring.
the maternal genotype and the epigenetic regulation in the fetus are two of the major factors that determine the phenotypes of FASD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the genetic and epigenomic mechanisms that contribute to the variations of the alcohol-exposure phenotypes are not independent of one another, rather, they interact to modulate the vulnerability and resilience of the alcohol-exposures.
the genetic and epigenetics of FASD are not only a matter of maternal and paternal alleles, but are also a matter of the interaction of the alleles of each parent with one another.

the maternal and paternal genetic contributions, in conjunction with the epigenetic regulation in the alcohol-exposed offspring, can interact to modulate the vulnerability and resilience of the individual with FASD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the genetic and epigenetics of the maternal parent can interact with the genetic inheritance of the fetus to produce variations in the phenotype of the alcohol-exposure offspring.

the genetic and epigenetically regulated maternal contributions to the fetal phenotype, in addition to the paternal genetic contributions, must be accounted for when considering the severity of FASD symptomology.
the genetic and epigenomic factors interact in complex ways to modulate the vulnerability to alcohol exposure in the fetus.
